intro.html: Every story, storm and business has a start, and English has a crowd of words for it. Three are verbs for starting: commence, initiate and inaugurate. Three are nouns for the start itself: inception, genesis and onset. Four are adjectives for things that have only just begun: nascent, incipient, fledgling and rudimentary.

Listen for tone. Onset and incipient usually announce something unwelcome (the onset of a storm, an incipient leak). Nascent and fledgling are hopeful: something new is growing. Inaugurate means a formal ceremony.

words.def: to begin, especially in a formal way
words.ex: The concert will {commence} at seven o’clock sharp.
words.ctx: Once the judge entered and everyone was seated, the trial could finally {commence}, three hours later than planned.
words.etym: From Old French comencier, from Latin com- + initiare (to begin).
words.note: A graduation is called a commencement because it begins the graduates’ new lives.

mn.cue: COMMENCEMENT: the day your new life BEGINS
mn.text: Graduation is called commencement because it is a beginning, not an end. On that day, the graduates {commence} their grown-up lives.

scene.alt: Two graduates in caps cheer under falling confetti on graduation day.

words.def: to set something going; also, to admit a new member to a group
words.ex: Zoe {initiated} the dancing by stepping onto the empty floor.
words.ctx: No one wanted to be the first to apologize, so the twins sat in silence until their little brother {initiated} peace talks with a plate of cookies.
words.etym: From Latin initiare, “to begin, admit,” from initium, “a beginning.”

mn.text: At the party everyone stands around shyly until Zoe takes the initial step onto the dance floor. She {initiates} the dancing.

scene.alt: A girl starts dancing first at a party while two shy friends watch.

words.def: to open or begin with a formal ceremony; to install in office
words.ex: The town {inaugurated} its new library with a ribbon, a band and a cake.
words.ctx: The railway was {inaugurated} with great fanfare: flags flew, a band played and the first train carried two hundred cheering guests.
words.etym: From Latin inaugurare, “to install after reading the omens,” from augur, a Roman official who read signs in the flight of birds.

mn.text: In August the town opens its new bridge with a band, balloons and a speech by Granny Mae. They {inaugurate} it.

scene.alt: A grandmother cheers under a grand opening banner as a boy drums beside the new bridge.

words.def: the moment at which something is founded or begun
words.ex: From its {inception}, the bakery was famous for its cinnamon rolls.
words.ctx: The festival has grown enormously since its {inception} in 1990, when a dozen neighbors set up card tables in a parking lot.
words.etym: From Latin inceptio, “a beginning,” from incipere, “to begin, take in hand”: in + capere (to take).

mn.cue: IN-CEPT-ion: the moment the idea is TAKEN IN
mn.text: Lin bites into her grandmother’s bread and cries, “I’ll open a bakery!” That moment was the bakery’s {inception}.

scene.alt: A woman tastes her grandmother’s bread and gets the idea to open a bakery.

words.def: the origin or birth of something
words.ex: The {genesis} of the giant oak was a single acorn.
words.ctx: The {genesis} of the town’s famous fall fair was a single bake sale, held by three friends on a rainy afternoon fifty years ago.
words.etym: From Greek genesis, “origin, birth,” related to gignesthai (to be born).

mn.text: Sami waters a tiny sprout beside the giant old oak. Every great tree has its {genesis}, its birth, in one small seed.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to water a tiny sprout that stands near a giant oak tree.

words.def: the beginning of something, usually something unpleasant
words.ex: At the {onset} of the storm, the picnickers grabbed their baskets and ran.
words.ctx: With the {onset} of winter, the birds that had crowded the feeder all summer flew south, and the garden grew silent.

mn.text: The sky darkens and the first raindrops fall: the storm is setting on. At its {onset}, the picnickers grab their baskets and run.

scene.alt: Picnickers run with a basket and an umbrella as a storm begins.

words.def: just born; only beginning to exist or grow
words.ex: With six teams and one muddy field, the town’s {nascent} soccer league was only a few weeks old.
words.ctx: The club was still {nascent}, with only six members and no meeting room, but its founders had big plans for the year ahead.
words.etym: From Latin nascens, “being born,” from nasci (to be born), the same root as native and nature.

mn.text: The chick has just pecked its way out of the shell, and its life has only begun. Something that new is {nascent}.

scene.alt: A just-hatched chick peeps out of its nest as the mother hen looks on lovingly.

words.def: just beginning to appear or develop, often as an early sign of trouble
words.ex: Dad spotted the {incipient} leak while it was still a single drip.
words.ctx: The dentist caught the {incipient} cavity early, when it was only a tiny gray spot, and filled it before it could ever hurt.
words.etym: From Latin incipiens, “beginning,” from incipere (to begin): in + capere (to take).
words.note: Close to nascent, but incipient often warns of something unwelcome: an incipient crack, an incipient cold.

mn.cue: IN-SIP-ient: the first little SIP of trouble
mn.text: A single drip from the ceiling is the first little sip of a leak. Fix it now, while the leak is still {incipient}, before the roof gives way.

scene.alt: A worried man points up at a drip from the ceiling falling into a bucket.

words.def: new and inexperienced, like a young bird learning to fly
words.ex: The {fledgling} pilot gripped the controls nervously on her very first solo flight.
words.ctx: The {fledgling} theater company had no stage of its own yet, so its first play was performed in a borrowed barn with hay bales for seats.
words.etym: From fledge, “to grow the feathers needed to fly,” + -ling, as in duckling.

mn.cue: a FLEDGLING bird: first wobbly flight
mn.text: Like a baby bird on its first wobbly flight, Kai’s brand-new lemonade stand is just getting started. It is a {fledgling} business.

scene.alt: A boy runs a new lemonade stand as a baby bird wobbles through its first flight overhead.

words.def: basic and simple; not developed beyond the first stage
words.ex: Pip’s first treehouse was {rudimentary}: four boards and a blanket for a roof.
words.ctx: The travelers spoke only {rudimentary} French, enough to order bread and ask for the station, but not enough to follow the guide’s long stories.
words.etym: From rudiment, from Latin rudimentum, “a first attempt,” from rudis (rough, unformed).

mn.text: Pip’s first treehouse is rough and simple: four boards, a rope and a blanket for a roof. It is {rudimentary}.

scene.alt: A proud boy stands by a tree with a single board nailed up as his simple treehouse.

head: part of speech
words
notes
rows: incipient often warns; fledgling = new and untested; rudimentary = basic
after.cap: Words for starts, sorted by part of speech.

after.html: Fledgling comes from a young bird that has just grown the feathers to fly. A fledgling business, like the bird, is new, wobbly and still learning.

items.q: Which phrase uses incipient the way writers usually do?
choices: an incipient crack in the dam
an incipient prize for the winner
an incipient ending to the story
items.why: Incipient usually describes something unwelcome that is just beginning, like a crack that could grow.

items.q: The city held a ribbon-cutting, a parade and speeches to ______ the new bridge.
items.why: To inaugurate is to open or begin with a formal ceremony. The other words are not verbs.

choices: the onset of a lovely vacation
the onset of my birthday gift
items.why: Onset usually names the start of something unpleasant, such as an illness or a storm.

items.q: True or false: a fledgling company has been in business for a hundred years.
items.why: False. Fledgling means new and inexperienced, like a young bird just learning to fly.
